title: The Higgs boson
seal: The origin of mass, in Brussels and Edinburgh
reading: This envelope reaches far. After your theory is joined to relativity and applied to fields, physicists will build a 'Standard Model' of the fundamental particles and their interactions. In 1964 François Englert and Robert Brout — here in Brussels — and independently Peter Higgs in Edinburgh, and others, will propose a mechanism by which a field pervading space gives mass to particles that would otherwise have none. It predicts a new particle. In July 2012, at a laboratory near Geneva, two experiments colliding protons at energies millions of times those of your X-rays announce a new boson with a mass about 133 times that of the hydrogen atom. The 2013 Nobel Prize goes to Englert and Higgs; Brout had died in 2011.
detail: The particle's mass is about 125 GeV. The mechanism allows the carriers of the weak nuclear force to be massive while preserving the gauge symmetry of the theory. It answers an objection Pauli raised in 1953–54 to massless gauge fields.

claim.label: Fields all the way down
claim.summary: Inference: Dirac's 1927 quantisation of the radiation field is the ancestor of this framework.
voice: If light quanta are excitations of a quantised field, I see no reason why every particle should not be. A field that fills space and gives the others mass is strange, but not stranger than the radiation field was two years ago.

claim.label: The mass problem
claim.summary: Pauli in 1953–54 objected that gauge fields of the Yang–Mills type would have massless quanta. The 1927 Pauli cannot know this; his demand for mathematical consistency is documented.
voice: A field that fills all of space, whose only work is to give other particles their mass? I should want to see that the mathematics holds together before I believe the laboratory — and then I should want the laboratory.
claim.later: Pauli's objection to massless gauge quanta, raised against Yang in 1954, is exactly what this mechanism resolves.

claim.label: The scale of the laboratory
claim.summary: Speculative; grounded in Curie's experience of building a laboratory.
voice: Pierre and I found radium in a shed. You tell me this needed a machine many kilometres around and thousands of people. I believe the result the way I believe any careful measurement — and I should very much like to see the machine.

claim.label: And gravity?
claim.summary: Speculative; grounded in Einstein's documented pursuit of a unified field theory.
voice: A complete account of the particles — except gravitation, I assume? Then it is not yet complete in the sense I care about.
